We give the argument in full, because its structure differs from the anchored case: there is no
comparator subtraction to cancel a prognostic variable, so each absolute conditional mean must be
identified outright.

*Step 1 (identify the source conditional mean).* The arm-$A$ source IPD identifies the source-conditional
mean $\mu_A^{\mathrm{src}}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathrm{src}}[Y\mid T=A,\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}]$. Under
(i) this equals the target-conditional mean $\mu_A(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}^{*}}[Y(A)\mid
\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{x}]$. Assumption (i) is strong: it requires that, conditional on $\mathbf{x}$, no
variable left out of $\mathbf{x}$ shifts the absolute mean of $Y(A)$ between source and target; by (ii)
every imbalanced prognostic variable is in $\mathbf{x}$, which is what reduces (i) to within-population
unconfoundedness plus the absence of differentially distributed *unmeasured* prognostic variables.

*Step 2 (identify the target marginal mean).* By the g-formula (@thm-g-computation-unbiased),
$$
\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}^{*})}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim f_{*}}[\mu_A(\mathbf{X})]
=\int\mu_A(\mathbf{x})\,f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}.
$$

*Step 3 (the weighted estimator hits it).* MAIC reweights the source-$A$ IPD to match the target moments,
so by the affine-mean argument of Step 2 of @thm-anchored-maic-consistency, applied now to the *absolute*
mean rather than a contrast,
$$
\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}
=\frac{\sum_i w_i^{*}\,\mathbf{1}\{T_i=A\}\,Y_i}{\sum_i w_i^{*}\,\mathbf{1}\{T_i=A\}}
\xrightarrow{p}\int\mu_A(\mathbf{x})\,f_{*}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}=\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}^{*})}.
$$
Here is the decisive difference from the anchored case: the weighted mean must converge to the *absolute*
target mean $\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}^{*})}$, not to a difference of conditional means against a shared
comparator. There is no subtraction to cancel a prognostic variable, so the full conditional mean
function $\mu_A(\cdot)$, not merely the CATE $\tau(\cdot)$, must be transported, which is why (ii) demands
prognostic variables and not only effect modifiers.

*Step 4 (the other arm and the contrast).* When $\mathcal{P}^{*}$ is the $B$ population, the reported arm
mean $\hat\mu_B$ is consistent for $\bar\mu_{B(\mathcal{P}^{*})}$ directly; when $B$ also has IPD the
symmetric argument gives the same limit. By the continuous mapping theorem,
$$
\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,unanch}}=g(\hat\mu_B)-g(\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}})
\xrightarrow{p}g(\bar\mu_{B(\mathcal{P}^{*})})-g(\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}^{*})})=d_{AB(\mathcal{P}^{*})}.
\qquad\square
$$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why prognostic variables matter here but not in the anchored case.** In the anchored estimator the
quantity that enters is the CATE $\tau(\mathbf{x})=\mu_C(\mathbf{x})-\mu_A(\mathbf{x})$. If $w$ is a
prognostic variable for both $A$ and $C$ that is *not* an effect modifier on the chosen scale, then it
shifts $\mu_A(\mathbf{x},w)$ and $\mu_C(\mathbf{x},w)$ by the same amount, so it cancels in the
difference: $\mu_C(\mathbf{x},w)-\mu_A(\mathbf{x},w)=\mu_C(\mathbf{x})-\mu_A(\mathbf{x})$, and omitting
$w$ from $\mathbf{x}$ does not bias the anchored estimate. In the unanchored estimator the quantity that
enters is $\mu_A(\mathbf{x})$ *alone*. If $w$ is an omitted prognostic variable for $A$, then
$\mu_A(\mathbf{x},w)$ depends on $w$, and integrating it against the source's $f(w\mid\mathbf{x})$ rather
than the target's $f^{*}(w\mid\mathbf{x})$ gives a different answer; the absolute mean is biased. This is
the formal reason that unanchored population adjustment requires strictly more covariate coverage than
anchored, and it is identical in form to the baseline-cancellation argument of @prp-baseline-cancellation
in Chapter 14: the anchor cancels the baseline; without it the baseline must be modeled.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Practical defensibility.** Conditional constancy of absolute effects (i) is essentially untestable in
the two-study setting (@prp-testable-untestable-constancy), and the adjustment set demanded by (ii), every
imbalanced effect modifier *and* prognostic variable, is usually prohibitive. For these reasons
@phillippo2016tsd18 treats unanchored comparisons as a last resort, to be accompanied by extensive
sensitivity analysis over the adjustment set. On non-collapsible scales the target marginal contrast also
depends on the target baseline risk, a further complication (@thm-sema-insufficient); the systematic
remedy is multilevel unanchored meta-regression (Chapter 26). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This result corresponds to F.7 in the proof catalogue.

## The effective sample size and its bound {#sec-maic-ess}

Reweighting is not free. A weighted estimator behaves, for the purpose of variance, like an unweighted
estimator on a *smaller* sample, and the size of that smaller sample is the effective sample size.

::: {#def-maic-ess}
## Effective sample size
For nonnegative weights $w_1,\dots,w_n$, not all zero, the **effective sample size** is
$$
\mathrm{ESS}\;:=\;\frac{\big(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i\big)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i^2}.
$$ {#eq-maic-ess}
It is invariant to rescaling all weights by a common positive constant. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

*Reader translation.* Read the ESS as "how many equally weighted patients this weighted sample is worth."
If you threw away your weighted sample of $n$ patients and replaced it with $\mathrm{ESS}$ fresh patients,
each counted once, you would get an estimate of the same precision. When the weights are equal the two are
the same and $\mathrm{ESS}=n$; when a few patients carry most of the weight the sample is effectively much
smaller, because the estimate leans on those few. The following table makes the collapse concrete for the
four-patient running example; notice how emphasis concentrating onto one patient drives the ESS toward $1$.

| Weights ($n=4$) | Situation | $\mathrm{ESS}$ | $\mathrm{ESS}/n$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(1,1,1,1)$ | uniform (no adjustment) | $4.00$ | $1.00$ |
| $(1.5,1.5,0.5,0.5)$ | running @exm-maic-running (one covariate matched) | $3.20$ | $0.80$ |
| $(2.25,0.75,0.75,0.25)$ | @sec-maic-example (two covariates matched) | $2.56$ | $0.64$ |
| $(2.5,0.5,0.5,0.5)$ | one patient dominant | $2.29$ | $0.57$ |
| $(4,0,0,0)$ | all weight on one patient | $1.00$ | $0.25$ |

::: {#thm-maic-ess-bound}
## The effective-sample-size bound
For any nonnegative weights $w_1,\dots,w_n$, not all zero,
$$
\mathrm{ESS}=\frac{\big(\sum_i w_i\big)^2}{\sum_i w_i^2}\;\le\;n,
$$
with equality if and only if all the weights are equal.

[machine-checked: `theories/MAIC.v`, `Theorem ESS_upper_bound`]
:::

::: {.proof}
This is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality (Chapter 2) applied to the vectors $\mathbf{w}=(w_1,\dots,w_n)$ and
$\mathbf{1}_n=(1,\dots,1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$:
$$
\Big(\sum_i w_i\Big)^2=\langle\mathbf{w},\mathbf{1}_n\rangle^2
\le\|\mathbf{w}\|_2^2\,\|\mathbf{1}_n\|_2^2=\Big(\sum_i w_i^2\Big)\cdot n.
$$
Dividing by $\sum_i w_i^2>0$ gives $\mathrm{ESS}\le n$. We exhibit the bound and its equality case
self-containedly through Lagrange's identity, which makes the slack explicit:
$$
n\sum_i w_i^2-\Big(\sum_i w_i\Big)^2
=\sum_{i}\sum_{j}w_i^2-\sum_i\sum_j w_iw_j
=\tfrac12\sum_{i}\sum_{j}\big(w_i^2-2w_iw_j+w_j^2\big)
=\sum_{i<j}(w_i-w_j)^2\ge 0,
$$
where the second equality writes $n\sum_i w_i^2=\sum_j\sum_i w_i^2$ and uses the symmetry of the double
sum under interchange of $i$ and $j$ to symmetrize. The right-hand side is a sum of squares, hence
nonnegative, which gives $(\sum_i w_i)^2\le n\sum_i w_i^2$ and therefore $\mathrm{ESS}\le n$; it vanishes
if and only if $w_i=w_j$ for all pairs $i<j$, that is, if and only if all weights are equal. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The Coq proof.** The companion development proves this bound without admissions. The elementary
inequality $2xy\le x^2+y^2$ is `Lemma two_mul_le_sqr` (a rearrangement of $0\le(x-y)^2$); an induction on
$n$ assembles it into the Cauchy-Schwarz statement $(\sum_i w_i)^2\le n\sum_i w_i^2$, named
`cauchy_schwarz_ones` in its general form and `cauchy_schwarz_n_weights` specialized to the weight
vector; dividing by the positive $\sum_i w_i^2$ yields `Theorem ESS_upper_bound`. The inductive step is
exactly the symmetrization used in Lagrange's identity above. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The bound is what gives the ESS its meaning as a sample size: the most informative weighting, uniform
weighting, retains all $n$ observations, and any departure strictly reduces the effective count.

This result corresponds to F.8 in the proof catalogue.

## Variance inflation {#sec-maic-variance}

The effective sample size is not a metaphor; it is the literal denominator in the variance of a weighted
mean.

::: {#thm-maic-variance-inflation}
## Variance of a weighted mean and the inflation factor
Let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be uncorrelated with common mean $\theta$ and common variance $\sigma^2$, and let
$w_1,\dots,w_n\ge 0$ be fixed weights, not all zero. The weighted mean
$\hat\theta_w=\sum_i w_iY_i/\sum_i w_i$ is unbiased for $\theta$ and has variance
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_w)=\sigma^2\,\frac{\sum_i w_i^2}{(\sum_i w_i)^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{\mathrm{ESS}}.
$$ {#eq-maic-var-weighted}
Consequently its variance is the unweighted variance $\sigma^2/n$ inflated by the factor
$$
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_w)}{\sigma^2/n}=\frac{n}{\mathrm{ESS}}\;\ge\;1,
$$ {#eq-maic-inflation}
with equality if and only if the weights are uniform (@thm-maic-ess-bound).
:::

::: {.proof}
Unbiasedness is linearity of expectation: $\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_w]=\sum_i w_i\theta/\sum_i w_i=\theta$.
For the variance, the $Y_i$ are uncorrelated with variance $\sigma^2$, so
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_w)
=\frac{1}{(\sum_i w_i)^2}\sum_i w_i^2\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)
=\frac{\sigma^2\sum_i w_i^2}{(\sum_i w_i)^2}
=\frac{\sigma^2}{\mathrm{ESS}},
$$
which is @eq-maic-var-weighted. Dividing by $\sigma^2/n$ gives the inflation factor
$n/\mathrm{ESS}$, and $n/\mathrm{ESS}\ge 1$ is the bound @thm-maic-ess-bound, with the same equality
condition. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The fundamental MAIC trade-off.** Equation @eq-maic-inflation is the quantitative form of the central
tension in population adjustment. Balancing more covariates, or balancing a fixed set more tightly against
a distant target, reduces bias but spreads the weights and lowers the ESS, inflating the variance:
$\mathrm{ESS}=n/2$ doubles the variance, $\mathrm{ESS}=n/10$ tenfolds it, equivalent to discarding ninety
percent of the data. A common rule of thumb flags $\mathrm{ESS}/n<0.5$ as substantial information loss and
$\mathrm{ESS}/n<0.1$ as an analysis dominated by a handful of patients. Because the weights are in fact
estimated, @eq-maic-var-weighted is the leading term of the true variance; the honest variance that
accounts for weight estimation is the sandwich of @thm-maic-sandwich-variance, and the bias-variance
trade-off resurfaces in the simulation theory of Chapter 29. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This result corresponds to F.9 in the proof catalogue.

## MAIC cannot extrapolate {#sec-maic-noextrap}

*The punchline first.* Suppose the comparator $BC$ trial enrolled patients aged $75$ to $85$, but your
index $AC$ trial enrolled no one over $70$. Then MAIC cannot tell you what treatment $A$ does at age $80$,
no matter how cleverly the weights are chosen, because you have no patients there to reweight. Reweighting
can only shift emphasis among patients you already observed; it cannot conjure a treatment effect in a
region of covariate space your trial never entered. This section proves that this is not a shortcoming of a
particular estimator but a hard identification barrier: the target quantity is simply not determined by the
data MAIC uses. The remedy is to *model* the effect across covariate space, which is what simulated
treatment comparison (Chapter 19) and multilevel network meta-regression (Chapter 20) do, at the cost of a
parametric assumption MAIC avoids.

Overlap is not merely a regularity condition for finite weights; it is a hard limit on what reweighting
can ever learn. If the target population places mass where the IPD never looked, no choice of finite
weights can recover the missing information, and the target estimand is not identified from the data MAIC
uses.

::: {#thm-maic-no-extrapolation}
## Non-identification beyond the covariate support
Suppose there is a measurable region $\mathcal{X}_0\subseteq\mathcal{X}$ with positive target probability
but zero index support,
$$
P_{\mathcal{P}_{BC}}(\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{X}_0)>0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
P_{\mathcal{P}_{AC}}(\mathbf{X}\in\mathcal{X}_0)=0.
$$
Then the comparator-population contrast $d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}$ is not identified from the index IPD
law of $(\mathbf{X},T,Y)$ together with the comparator density $f_{BC}$: there exist two data-generating
processes with identical index laws and identical $f_{BC}$ but different
$d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}$. In particular, no estimator that is a functional of the index empirical
distribution and the comparator moments, and so no finite-weight MAIC estimator @eq-maic-anchored-est, can
be consistent for $d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}$ across all such processes.
:::

::: {.proof}
The target contrast decomposes over the support gap. On the identity scale (the argument is identical on
any scale after applying $g$), with CATE $\tau(\mathbf{x})=\mu_A(\mathbf{x})-\mu_C(\mathbf{x})$,
$$
d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=\int_{\mathcal{X}\setminus\mathcal{X}_0}\tau(\mathbf{x})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
+\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}\tau(\mathbf{x})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}.
$$ {#eq-maic-nonid}
The first integral is over the region the index trial observes and is a functional of the index law and
$f_{BC}$; the second integral is over $\mathcal{X}_0$, where the index trial contributes no observations.

To prove non-identification, construct two processes that agree on everything observable yet differ in
@eq-maic-nonid. Let the index law of $(\mathbf{X},T,Y)$ and the comparator density $f_{BC}$ be fixed.
Choose two conditional-contrast functions $\tau_1,\tau_2$ that coincide on the index support
$\operatorname{supp}(f_{AC})\subseteq\mathcal{X}\setminus\mathcal{X}_0$ but differ on $\mathcal{X}_0$ in a
way that changes the gap integral, that is
$$
\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}\tau_1(\mathbf{x})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x}
\neq\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}\tau_2(\mathbf{x})\,f_{BC}(\mathbf{x})\,d\mathbf{x};
$$
such functions exist because $f_{BC}$ has positive mass on $\mathcal{X}_0$, so the linear functional
$\tau\mapsto\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}\tau f_{BC}$ is not identically zero on functions supported in
$\mathcal{X}_0$. Because $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ agree on $\operatorname{supp}(f_{AC})$ and the index trial
never visits $\mathcal{X}_0$, the two processes induce the *same* index law of $(\mathbf{X},T,Y)$ and the
same $f_{BC}$; yet by @eq-maic-nonid their values of $d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}$ differ by the nonzero
amount $\int_{\mathcal{X}_0}(\tau_1-\tau_2)f_{BC}$. Hence the contrast is not a function of the observable
law, which is non-identification. Any estimator built from the index empirical distribution and the
comparator moments, MAIC included, takes the same value under the two processes and so is inconsistent
for at least one of them. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reweighting interpolates, it does not extrapolate.** A finite-weight estimator outputs a weighted
combination of the observed conditional contrasts $\{\tau(\mathbf{x}_i)\}$, which can only land in their
convex hull; it has no mechanism to report a value of $\tau$ at an unobserved $\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}_0$.
This is the population-level shadow of the convex-hull feasibility condition @eq-maic-feasible-hull: when
$\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}$ escapes the hull, the weights diverge (@thm-maic-existence-uniqueness), and the
missing-mass integral in @eq-maic-nonid is exactly what the divergence is failing to capture. The remedy
is not a better weighting but a model: an outcome model that *interpolates* $\tau$ across covariate space,
which is what simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19) and multilevel network meta-regression
(Chapter 20) provide, at the cost of a parametric assumption that MAIC avoids. Diagnostics should compare
the index and comparator covariate ranges before any MAIC is attempted. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This result corresponds to F.10 in the proof catalogue.

## Standard errors: the sandwich {#sec-maic-sandwich}

*The one-line rule for practice.* Do not compute your standard errors as if the weights were known numbers.
You chose the weights by fitting them to the very same patients whose outcomes you are now averaging, and
pretending otherwise misstates the uncertainty, in a direction that depends on the data. The two honest options are the sandwich
variance developed here and the bootstrap of @sec-maic-bootstrap; the naive fixed-weight standard error is
not one of them.

The estimated weights make the naive variance @eq-maic-var-weighted wrong: it treats the weights as fixed
when they were in fact fitted to the same data. The honest variance treats the entire procedure, weight
fitting and outcome averaging, as a single system of estimating equations and applies the M-estimation
sandwich of Chapter 5 (@def-sandwich-variance).

Stack the parameters as $\boldsymbol{\theta}=(\boldsymbol{\beta},\mu_A,\mu_C)$ and define the per-patient
estimating function $\boldsymbol{\psi}(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta})$ with three blocks: the balance
block, which fits $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, and the two outcome blocks, which fit the weighted arm means,
$$
\boldsymbol{\psi}(\mathbf{x}_i,T_i,Y_i;\boldsymbol{\theta})
=\begin{pmatrix}
e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i}\,\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i\\[2pt]
\mathbf{1}\{T_i=A\}\,e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i}\,(Y_i-\mu_A)\\[2pt]
\mathbf{1}\{T_i=C\}\,e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i}\,(Y_i-\mu_C)
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\boldsymbol{\psi}(\mathbf{x}_i,T_i,Y_i;\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\mathbf{0}.
$$ {#eq-maic-estfun}
The first block is the balance condition @eq-maic-balance-beta; the second and third define
$\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}$ and $\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}$ of @eq-maic-ht. The normalization constant
$\alpha$ does not appear in the balance block because it multiplies the whole balance equation by the
positive factor $e^{\alpha}$, which cannot change whether that equation equals zero; only
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is a free parameter to be fit here, and $\alpha$ is recovered afterward from the
normalization (@eq-maic-alpha).

::: {#thm-maic-sandwich-variance}
## Sandwich variance for MAIC
Suppose the M-estimator $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ solving @eq-maic-estfun is consistent for
$\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ with the standard regularity conditions of Chapter 5 (the map
$\boldsymbol{\theta}\mapsto\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\psi}]$ is differentiable with nonsingular Jacobian
$A=\mathbb{E}[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\boldsymbol{\psi}(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)]$, and
$B=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\psi}\boldsymbol{\psi}^\top]$ is finite). Then
$$
\sqrt{n}\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)\xrightarrow{\ d\ }\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\,
\mathbb{V}),\qquad \mathbb{V}=A^{-1}B\,A^{-\top},
$$ {#eq-maic-sandwich}
the sandwich variance of @def-sandwich-variance, consistently estimated by
$\hat{\mathbb{V}}=\hat A^{-1}\hat B\,\hat A^{-\top}$ with
$\hat A=\tfrac1n\sum_i\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\boldsymbol{\psi}_i$ and
$\hat B=\tfrac1n\sum_i\boldsymbol{\psi}_i\boldsymbol{\psi}_i^\top$ evaluated at
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$. The asymptotic variance of the adjusted contrast
$\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=g(\hat\mu_C)-g(\hat\mu_A)$ follows by the delta method, and that of the
anchored estimator @eq-maic-anchored-est by adding the independent variance of
$\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\tfrac1n\sum_i\boldsymbol{\psi}(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta})$, so that
$M_n(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})=\mathbf{0}$ and
$M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta})\to M(\boldsymbol{\theta})=\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{\psi}]$ with
$M(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)=\mathbf{0}$. By a first-order Taylor expansion of $M_n$ about
$\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$, with $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ on the segment between
$\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ and $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$,
$$
\mathbf{0}=M_n(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}})
=M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)+\nabla M_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0).
$$
By the law of large numbers $\nabla M_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\xrightarrow{p}A$ (using consistency
of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ and continuity of the Jacobian), and $A$ is nonsingular by hypothesis, so
for large $n$ it may be inverted:
$$
\sqrt{n}\,(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)
=-\big(\nabla M_n(\tilde{\boldsymbol{\theta}})\big)^{-1}\sqrt{n}\,M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)
=-A^{-1}\sqrt{n}\,M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)+o_p(1).
$$
By the central limit theorem, $\sqrt{n}\,M_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)=\tfrac1{\sqrt n}\sum_i
\boldsymbol{\psi}(\,\cdot\,;\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},B)$ since the
summands are independent and identically distributed with mean $M(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)=\mathbf{0}$ and
covariance $B$. Slutsky's theorem then gives
$\sqrt{n}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}-\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)\xrightarrow{d}-A^{-1}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},B)
=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},A^{-1}BA^{-\top})$, which is @eq-maic-sandwich. Consistency of
$\hat{\mathbb{V}}=\hat A^{-1}\hat B\hat A^{-\top}$ is the law of large numbers applied to $\hat A$ and
$\hat B$ together with continuity of matrix inversion. The delta method (the smooth-map asymptotics of
Chapter 5, the same tool behind @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality) propagates @eq-maic-sandwich through
$g$ to the contrast, and the comparator term, being from a disjoint trial, contributes an additive
independent variance as in the Bucher variance (@thm-bucher-variance). $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why naive standard errors are wrong, structurally.** The Jacobian $A$ of @eq-maic-estfun is block
*lower-triangular*: the balance block depends only on $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, but the outcome blocks depend
on both $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and the means, since the weights $e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top
\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i}$ carry $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ into the outcome equations. Inverting a
block-triangular $A$ propagates the sampling uncertainty of $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ into the variance
of $(\hat\mu_A,\hat\mu_C)$ through the off-diagonal block. A naive analysis that treats the weights as
fixed drops that off-diagonal block, that is, it pretends the balance block and the outcome blocks are
uncoupled; it therefore generally *misstates* the variance. Often the correction is negative: estimating
the weights removes the part of the outcome variation explained by the balanced covariates, as for the
calibration estimators of survey sampling (@deville1992), so fixed-weight standard errors tend to be
conservative. The sign is not universal (@exr-maic-sandwich-vs-naive), which is exactly why the full
sandwich, not a fixed-weight shortcut, is needed.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This result corresponds to F.11 in the proof catalogue.

## Standard errors: the bootstrap {#sec-maic-bootstrap}

*The one-line rule for practice.* To bootstrap a MAIC, resample the index patients with replacement and
*refit the weights from scratch on every resample*, then recompute the adjusted contrast; the spread of
those recomputed contrasts is your standard error. The common mistake is to freeze the fitted weights and
resample only the outcomes, which quietly reproduces the wrong fixed-weight variance of @sec-maic-sandwich.
Refitting the weights each time is what lets the bootstrap feel the uncertainty in the weights themselves.

One technical term recurs below. A map $\Psi$ of the data distribution is **Hadamard-differentiable** when
it is smooth enough, in the functional sense used for the delta method in Chapter 5, that a small
perturbation of the input distribution produces an approximately linear change in the output; it is the
infinite-dimensional analogue of "differentiable," and it is exactly the condition under which resampling
the input (the bootstrap) correctly reproduces the sampling distribution of the output. (Fréchet
differentiability, mentioned in the proof, is a slightly stronger version of the same idea.)

The sandwich variance requires differentiating the estimating equations; the nonparametric bootstrap
sidesteps the algebra by resampling, and it is valid here because the whole MAIC map is smooth in the
empirical distribution.

::: {#thm-maic-bootstrap}
## Validity of the nonparametric bootstrap for MAIC
Let $\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\Psi(\mathbb{P}_n)$, where $\mathbb{P}_n$ is the empirical distribution
of the index IPD and $\Psi$ is the map that fits the entropy-balancing weights, forms the weighted arm
means, and returns the contrast. Under the regularity conditions of @thm-maic-sandwich-variance (in
particular overlap, so that the balance Jacobian
$\partial_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mathbb{E}[e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\Delta}}
\boldsymbol{\Delta}]$ is nonsingular at the solution), $\Psi$ is Hadamard-differentiable at the index law,
and therefore the nonparametric bootstrap is consistent: the bootstrap distribution of
$\sqrt{n}\big(\Psi(\mathbb{P}_n^{*})-\Psi(\mathbb{P}_n)\big)$ converges to the same limiting law as
$\sqrt{n}\big(\Psi(\mathbb{P}_n)-\Psi(\mathbb{P})\big)$, conditionally on the data and in probability.
Bootstrap percentile and studentized intervals are thus asymptotically valid.
:::

::: {.proof}
We verify the hypotheses of the functional delta method for the bootstrap (the named theorem we invoke is
Theorem 23.9 of @vandervaart1998), namely that $\Psi$ is a composition of Hadamard-differentiable maps of
the empirical distribution.

First, the weight parameter is a smooth functional of the law. Define
$\mathbf{G}(\boldsymbol{\beta},F)=\int e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})}
(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})\,dF(\mathbf{x})$; the fitted $\boldsymbol{\beta}(F)$ solves
$\mathbf{G}(\boldsymbol{\beta},F)=\mathbf{0}$, which is @eq-maic-balance-beta for $F=\mathbb{P}_n$. The
partial derivative
$\partial_{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\mathbf{G}=\int e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})}
(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})^\top\,dF$ is a positive multiple of a
covariance-type matrix and is nonsingular at the solution under overlap (it is $Z\cdot\nabla^2 Q$ in the
notation of @eq-maic-hess-q, positive definite when the centered covariates span). The implicit function
theorem then makes $\boldsymbol{\beta}(F)$ Fréchet-, hence Hadamard-, differentiable in $F$ along the
directions generated by empirical processes.

Second, given $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, the weighted arm means
$\mu_t(F,\boldsymbol{\beta})=\int\mathbf{1}\{T=t\}e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})}
y\,dF\big/\int\mathbf{1}\{T=t\}e^{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top(\mathbf{x}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC})}\,dF$ are ratios
of integrals against $F$ of functions indexed smoothly by $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, which form a Donsker class
under the finite second moments assumed in @thm-maic-sandwich-variance, hence Hadamard-differentiable in
$(F,\boldsymbol{\beta})$ wherever the denominator is bounded away from zero (guaranteed by positivity of
the weights, @thm-maic-exponential-weights). Third, the link $g$ and the subtraction are smooth maps of
the means. The composition $\Psi$ of Hadamard-differentiable maps is Hadamard-differentiable by the chain
rule for such maps (@vandervaart1998, Theorem 20.9).

By the empirical-process central limit theorem $\sqrt{n}(\mathbb{P}_n-\mathbb{P})$ converges to a
tight Gaussian process, and that same process governs the bootstrap empirical measure. The functional
delta method for the bootstrap (@vandervaart1998, Theorem 23.9) then transfers the convergence through the
Hadamard-differentiable $\Psi$: the bootstrapped statistic and the original statistic share the limiting
Gaussian law, which is precisely the sandwich law of @thm-maic-sandwich-variance. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Resample the whole procedure.** Validity requires bootstrapping the *entire* map $\Psi$, refitting the
weights on each resample, not freezing the weights and resampling only the outcomes; freezing the weights
reproduces the naive fixed-weight variance and inherits its bias (@thm-maic-sandwich-variance remark). The
bootstrap and the sandwich agree to first order and typically differ only by small-sample fluctuation; the
bootstrap is often preferred in practice because it sidesteps assembling the Jacobian blocks of
@eq-maic-estfun by hand, while the sandwich is cheaper when many bootstrap replicates would be costly.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

This result corresponds to F.12 in the proof catalogue.

## A fully worked two-covariate example {#sec-maic-example}

We carry a complete anchored MAIC from raw covariates to an adjusted indirect comparison, choosing the
numbers so that every weight, the effective sample size, and the adjusted contrast are exact and
checkable by hand. The example is genuinely two-dimensional, with one effect modifier and one purely
prognostic covariate, so it also exhibits the dividing line between covariates that must be balanced and
covariates whose balance is harmless but costly.

::: {#exm-maic-twocov}
## Anchored MAIC with one effect modifier and one prognostic covariate
The index trial $AC$ has, in each arm, four patients sitting at the corners of a centered square in
standardized covariate space,
$$
\mathbf{x}\in\big\{(1,1),\,(1,-1),\,(-1,1),\,(-1,-1)\big\},
$$
where $x_1$ is an effect modifier of the $A$-versus-$C$ benefit and $x_2$ is purely prognostic. The
index covariate mean is the center, $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{AC}=(0,0)$. The comparator trial $BC$ reports the
covariate mean
$$
\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{BC}=(0.5,\,0.5),
$$
so the index population is imbalanced against the comparator on both covariates. The outcome $Y$ is a
continuous severity score (lower is better) with conditional means, on the identity scale, given by
$$
\mu_C(\mathbf{x})=20+2x_1+2x_2,
\qquad
\mu_A(\mathbf{x})=\mu_C(\mathbf{x})-\big(4+x_1\big)=16+x_1+2x_2.
$$
Thus the conditional benefit of $A$ over $C$ is $\mu_C(\mathbf{x})-\mu_A(\mathbf{x})=4+x_1$, which
depends on the effect modifier $x_1$ but not on $x_2$; the prognostic covariate $x_2$ shifts both arms
equally and cancels in the contrast.

**Step 1: set up the balance equation.** The centered covariates are
$\boldsymbol{\Delta}_i=\mathbf{x}_i-(0.5,0.5)$, which span $\mathbb{R}^2$, and the target $(0.5,0.5)$ lies
strictly inside the square $\operatorname{conv}\{(\pm1,\pm1)\}=[-1,1]^2$, so by
@thm-maic-existence-uniqueness a unique finite positive weight vector exists. The weights have the form
$w(\mathbf{x})=\exp(\alpha+\beta_1(x_1-0.5)+\beta_2(x_2-0.5))$, and we must solve the balance condition
@eq-maic-balance-beta.

**Step 2: exploit symmetry.** The point set and the target are both invariant under swapping the two
coordinates, so the unique solution must satisfy $\beta_1=\beta_2=:\beta$. Then, up to the constant
$\alpha$, $w(\mathbf{x})\propto e^{\beta(x_1+x_2)}$, and the four corners take values $x_1+x_2\in
\{2,0,0,-2\}$. The weighted mean of $x_1$ is
$$
\frac{\sum w\,x_1}{\sum w}
=\frac{e^{2\beta}(1)+1(1)+1(-1)+e^{-2\beta}(-1)}{e^{2\beta}+1+1+e^{-2\beta}}
=\frac{e^{2\beta}-e^{-2\beta}}{e^{2\beta}+e^{-2\beta}+2}
=\frac{2\sinh 2\beta}{2\cosh 2\beta+2}=\tanh\beta,
$$
using $\sinh 2\beta=2\sinh\beta\cosh\beta$ and $\cosh 2\beta+1=2\cosh^2\beta$. Setting this equal to the
target $0.5$ gives $\tanh\beta=\tfrac12$, that is
$$
\beta=\operatorname{artanh}(0.5)=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1+0.5}{1-0.5}=\tfrac12\ln 3\approx 0.5493,
\qquad e^{2\beta}=3,\quad e^{-2\beta}=\tfrac13.
$$
By symmetry the weighted mean of $x_2$ is also $\tanh\beta=0.5$, so both moments are matched.

**Step 3: the explicit weights.** Up to scale the corner weights are proportional to
$e^{\beta(x_1+x_2)}\in\{3,\,1,\,1,\,\tfrac13\}$, summing to $3+1+1+\tfrac13=\tfrac{16}{3}$. Normalizing
the four pattern weights to sum to $4$ multiplies by $4/(16/3)=\tfrac34$:
$$
w_{(1,1)}=\tfrac94=2.25,\quad
w_{(1,-1)}=\tfrac34=0.75,\quad
w_{(-1,1)}=\tfrac34=0.75,\quad
w_{(-1,-1)}=\tfrac14=0.25.
$$ {#eq-maic-example-weights}
These sum to $4$, and one checks the balance directly: the weighted mean of $x_1$ is
$(2.25\cdot 1+0.75\cdot 1+0.75\cdot(-1)+0.25\cdot(-1))/4=2/4=0.5$, and likewise the weighted mean of
$x_2$ is $(2.25-0.75+0.75-0.25)/4=0.5$. The normalization multiplier follows from
$w_{(1,1)}=e^{\alpha}e^{\beta}=e^{\alpha}\sqrt3=2.25$, giving
$e^{\alpha}=2.25/\sqrt3=\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{4}$ and $\alpha=\tfrac32\ln 3-\ln 4\approx 0.2616$.

**Step 4: the effective sample size.** With the four pattern weights @eq-maic-example-weights,
$$
\sum_i w_i=4,\qquad
\sum_i w_i^2=2.25^2+0.75^2+0.75^2+0.25^2=5.0625+0.5625+0.5625+0.0625=6.25,
$$
so
$$
\mathrm{ESS}=\frac{4^2}{6.25}=\frac{16}{6.25}=2.56,\qquad \frac{\mathrm{ESS}}{n}=\frac{2.56}{4}=0.64.
$$
Matching both covariate means cost $36\%$ of the effective sample. The variance inflation factor is
$n/\mathrm{ESS}=4/2.56=1.5625$ (@thm-maic-variance-inflation), so a weighted arm mean has standard error
$\sqrt{1.5625}=1.25$ times the unweighted standard error, a $25\%$ increase. (The bound
$\mathrm{ESS}\le n$ of @thm-maic-ess-bound is comfortably respected.)

**Step 5: the weighted arm means.** The arm-$A$ outcomes at the four patterns are
$\mu_A(1,1)=19$, $\mu_A(1,-1)=15$, $\mu_A(-1,1)=17$, $\mu_A(-1,-1)=13$; the arm-$C$ outcomes are
$\mu_C(1,1)=24$, $\mu_C(1,-1)=20$, $\mu_C(-1,1)=20$, $\mu_C(-1,-1)=16$ (we set $Y$ equal to its
conditional mean to keep the arithmetic exact; with noise the estimator is consistent rather than exact,
@thm-anchored-maic-consistency). The weighted arm means are
$$
\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\frac{2.25(19)+0.75(15)+0.75(17)+0.25(13)}{4}=\frac{70}{4}=17.5,
$$
$$
\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\frac{2.25(24)+0.75(20)+0.75(20)+0.25(16)}{4}=\frac{88}{4}=22.
$$
Both equal the comparator-population truth: $\bar\mu_{A(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=16+0.5+2(0.5)=17.5$ and
$\bar\mu_{C(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=20+2(0.5)+2(0.5)=22$, confirming Step 2 of
@thm-anchored-maic-consistency.

**Step 6: the adjusted index contrast.** On the identity scale the benefit of $A$ over $C$ in the
comparator population is
$$
\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=\hat\mu_C^{\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat\mu_A^{\mathrm{MAIC}}=22-17.5=4.5,
$$
matching the true comparator-population benefit $4+\bar x_{1,BC}=4+0.5=4.5$. The *unadjusted* index
benefit, from the unweighted arm means $\bar\mu_A^{\mathrm{unw}}=(19+15+17+13)/4=16$ and
$\bar\mu_C^{\mathrm{unw}}=(24+20+20+16)/4=20$, is $20-16=4$, the benefit in the index population
($4+\bar x_{1,AC}=4+0=4$). MAIC has moved the estimate from $4$ to $4.5$, correcting for the higher value
of the effect modifier $x_1$ in the comparator population.

**Step 7: the anchored indirect comparison.** Suppose the comparator trial reports a $B$-versus-$C$
benefit of $\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}=3.0$ in its own population. The anchored MAIC estimate of the
$A$-versus-$B$ benefit in $\mathcal{P}_{BC}$ is
$$
\hat d_{AB}^{\mathrm{MAIC,anch}}=\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}-\hat d_{BC}^{\mathrm{AgD}}=4.5-3.0=1.5,
$$
the target estimand $d_{AB(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}=4.5-3.0=
1.5$. The *unadjusted* Bucher comparison would have used the index-population benefit $4.0$ and produced
$4.0-3.0=1.0$, biased by $-0.5$. The bias is exactly the effect-modification discrepancy
$d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{BC})}-d_{AC(\mathcal{P}_{AC})}=4.5-4.0=0.5$, caused by the imbalance in the effect
modifier $x_1$ ($\bar x_1=0.5$ in $\mathcal{P}_{BC}$ versus $0$ in $\mathcal{P}_{AC}$); this is precisely
the transitivity failure of @thm-failure-of-bucher that population adjustment removes. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the prognostic covariate cost.** The effect modifier $x_1$ *had* to be balanced: it drives the
$0.5$ bias correction. The prognostic covariate $x_2$ did *not* need balancing for the contrast, because
it cancels between the arms ($\mu_A$ and $\mu_C$ both carry $+2x_2$), yet we balanced it anyway, and doing
so contributed to the drop in effective sample size from $4$ to $2.56$. Had we balanced only $x_1$, the
weights would have been less variable and the ESS higher, at no cost in bias on the identity scale. This
is the anchored-case phenomenon of @thm-anchored-maic-consistency: only imbalanced effect modifiers are
mandatory; balancing pure prognostic variables is harmless for bias but spends precision. In the
unanchored case (@thm-unanchored-maic-consistency) the prognostic $x_2$ would *not* cancel, and balancing
it would be mandatory, which is one more reason the unanchored estimator is so much more expensive.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Practitioner checklist {#sec-maic-checklist}

The theory of this chapter condenses into a short list of things to do, and to check in someone else's
analysis, when performing or reviewing a MAIC. Each item names the result it rests on.

1. **Confirm overlap first.** Compare the comparator's reported covariate means (and ranges and standard
   deviations, when given) with the minimum and maximum in the index IPD. A comparator mean near or beyond
   an index extreme, or an optimizer that fails to converge or returns enormous weights, is an overlap
   failure, not a software glitch (@thm-maic-existence-uniqueness, @thm-maic-no-extrapolation).
2. **Balance every imbalanced effect modifier.** These are mandatory in both anchored and unanchored MAIC.
   On a nonlinear link (log odds ratio, log hazard ratio) balance higher moments as well, because
   first-moment matching is insufficient there (@exm-maic-logit-moments, @sec-maic-moment).
3. **Prefer anchored whenever a common comparator exists.** Anchored MAIC needs only effect modifiers;
   unanchored MAIC also needs every prognostic variable and rests on an untestable absolute-constancy
   assumption. Use unanchored only as a last resort, with sensitivity analysis over the adjustment set
   (@sec-maic-anchored, @sec-maic-unanchored).
4. **Report the effective sample size and flag low values.** State $\mathrm{ESS}$ and $\mathrm{ESS}/n$;
   treat $\mathrm{ESS}/n<0.5$ as substantial information loss and $\mathrm{ESS}/n<0.1$ as an analysis
   driven by a handful of patients. Show standardized covariate differences before and after weighting to
   confirm balance was achieved (@thm-maic-ess-bound, @thm-maic-variance-inflation).
5. **Use honest standard errors.** Compute uncertainty with the sandwich variance or a full bootstrap that
   refits the weights on each resample, never as if the weights were fixed; combine it with the published
   comparator effect's own standard error, which is independent (@thm-maic-sandwich-variance,
   @thm-maic-bootstrap).
6. **Mind the scale.** On non-collapsible scales, matching covariate means does not by itself make two
   marginal odds ratios or hazard ratios comparable; confirm that the scale-alignment conditions hold or
   move to a model-based method (@thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr, Chapter 20).

## Notes and references {#sec-maic-notes}

Matching-adjusted indirect comparison was introduced by @signorovitch2010maic, who proposed reweighting
the individual patient data of one trial so that its weighted baseline moments match those reported by a
comparator trial, and recognized the weights as inverse-odds weights from a logistic model of trial
membership. The entropy-balancing formulation, the derivation of the exponential weight form, the
convex-duality analysis of existence, the effective-sample-size diagnostic, and the placement of MAIC
within the anchored and unanchored population-adjustment framework follow the thesis of
@phillippo2019thesis and the NICE Decision Support Unit guidance @phillippo2016tsd18; the latter is the
standard practical reference for which covariates to balance, the anchored-versus-unanchored decision, and
the treatment of unanchored comparisons as a last resort. The maximum-entropy reading of covariate
balancing, with its exponential-family solution and its convex dual, is the entropy-balancing method
of @hainmueller2012 in the causal-inference literature; the equivalence between entropy balancing and a calibrated
logistic propensity model is a recurring theme there, and @thm-maic-logistic-ipw-equiv is its MAIC
instance, connected to the inverse-probability-weighting theory of Chapter 10 (@thm-ipw-unbiased,
@def-balancing-score) and the transportability theory of Chapter 12 (@def-transportability,
@thm-conditional-transportability).

The convex-analytic facts underlying @thm-maic-existence-uniqueness, that the gradient of a log-partition
function maps onto the relative interior of the convex hull of the sufficient statistics and that the
infimum is attained exactly when the origin lies in that relative interior, are standard in the theory of
exponential families and convex duality; the coercivity argument given here is self-contained and avoids
appealing to the general machinery of Rockafellar's *Convex Analysis*. The effective-sample-size bound
@thm-maic-ess-bound is the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and the variance interpretation @eq-maic-var-weighted
is the classical effective-sample-size formula for weighted means; both appear as Eq. (6.1) of
@phillippo2019thesis. The non-extrapolation theorem @thm-maic-no-extrapolation is the population-adjustment
form of a positivity or overlap requirement, and its failure under poor covariate overlap is documented in
the simulation studies of @phillippo2019thesis; the contrast with model-based methods that can interpolate
motivates simulated treatment comparison (Chapter 19) and multilevel network meta-regression
(Chapter 20). The sandwich variance @thm-maic-sandwich-variance is M-estimation theory applied to the
stacked weight-and-outcome equations (@def-sandwich-variance), and the bootstrap validity
@thm-maic-bootstrap is the functional delta method for the bootstrap (@vandervaart1998, Theorems 20.9,
23.9). The distinction between consistency and finite-sample unbiasedness, emphasized throughout
@sec-maic-anchored and @sec-maic-unanchored, corrects a looseness in some of the early MAIC literature; it
matters because the weights are estimated.

The companion Coq development formalizes the algebraic core of MAIC in `theories/MAIC.v`. The weight
function $w(\mathbf{x})=\exp(\text{linear predictor})$ is `maic_weight_fn`, proved positive in
`maic_weight_pos`; the effective sample size is `ESS`, and the bound $\mathrm{ESS}\le n$ is
`Theorem ESS_upper_bound`, the machine-checked counterpart of @thm-maic-ess-bound. Its proof is built from
the elementary `two_mul_le_sqr` ($2xy\le x^2+y^2$), assembled by induction into `cauchy_schwarz_ones` and
its weight specialization `cauchy_schwarz_n_weights`, and the development records no admissions for these
results. The anchored and unanchored estimators appear as `effect_AC_MAIC` and `effect_AB_anchored`, with
the substantive consistency content (@thm-anchored-maic-consistency, @thm-unanchored-maic-consistency)
carried by named section hypotheses standing for conditional constancy, complete effect-modifier coverage,
shared effect modification, and overlap, rather than as formalized probabilistic theorems; the
optimization that fixes $(\alpha,\boldsymbol{\beta})$ in @thm-maic-exponential-weights is likewise
pen-and-paper. Chapter 30 walks through `MAIC.v` in detail.

This chapter corresponds to results F.1 (method-of-moments balance), F.2 (the entropy objective), F.3 (the
exponential weights), F.4 (existence and uniqueness), F.5 (the logistic-IPW equivalence), F.6 (anchored
consistency), F.7 (unanchored consistency), F.8 (the ESS bound), F.9 (variance inflation), F.10 (the
no-extrapolation theorem), F.11 (the sandwich variance), and F.12 (bootstrap validity) of the proof
catalogue in `proofs/F_maic.md`. The general population-adjustment theory that MAIC specializes,
conditional constancy in its relative and absolute forms (@def-conditional-constancy-relative,
@def-conditional-constancy-absolute), the shared-effect-modifier assumption (@def-sema), and the anchored
and unanchored PAIC consistency theorems (@thm-anchored-paic-consistency, @thm-unanchored-paic-consistency),
is developed in Chapter 17. The regression-based alternative to reweighting, simulated treatment
comparison, and its asymptotic equivalence to MAIC under a correctly specified linear outcome model
(@thm-maic-stc-equivalence), is the subject of Chapter 19.

## Exercises {#sec-maic-exercises}

Throughout, a starred exercise, marked $\star$, has a full worked solution in Appendix F. The first three
exercises are warm-ups and interpretation checks that need only the ideas of this chapter; the later ones
build toward the proofs, and the two starred ones are the most demanding.

::: {#exr-maic-interpret-weights}
**Reading the weights.** *(Warm-up.)* In the running @exm-maic-running the two severe patients received
weight $1.5$ each and the two mild patients weight $0.5$ each. (a) In one sentence, say what a weight of
$1.5$ means for a severe patient, in terms of how many target-population patients they stand in for.
(b) Why are the severe patients upweighted rather than the mild ones, given that the comparator trial was
sicker? (c) Recompute the effective sample size from these weights and state, in plain words, how many
equally weighted patients this reweighted sample is worth. (d) Balancing a *second* imbalanced covariate
adds a constraint. Explain why the minimized entropy objective cannot decrease, and why the ESS typically,
though not necessarily, falls.
:::

::: {#exr-maic-em-vs-pv}
**Effect modifier or prognostic variable?** *(Interpretation.)* For each covariate below, state whether it
is most naturally an effect modifier, a prognostic variable, or both, and then say whether an *anchored*
MAIC and an *unanchored* MAIC would each be obliged to balance it, assuming it is imbalanced between the
trials. (a) A biomarker that predicts worse outcomes on every treatment but does not change the size of
$A$'s benefit over $C$. (b) Disease severity, which both worsens outcomes and enlarges the benefit of $A$.
(c) A covariate perfectly balanced between the two trials. Justify each answer in one sentence using the
cancellation argument of @sec-maic-anchored.
:::

::: {#exr-maic-diagnose-report}
**Judging a published MAIC.** *(Interpretation.)* A submission reports an *unanchored* MAIC comparing drug
$A$ (from an IPD trial of $n=400$ patients) against drug $B$, balancing three covariates, with an effective
sample size $\mathrm{ESS}=28$ and a $95\%$ confidence interval computed as though the weights were fixed.
The comparator's reported mean for one of the three covariates lies just above the largest value observed
in the IPD. List, in order of severity, the credibility concerns you would raise, and name the result of
this chapter behind each. (Consider at least: the anchored-versus-unanchored choice, the overlap of that
one covariate, the $\mathrm{ESS}/n$ ratio, and the variance method.)
:::

::: {#exr-maic-onecov}
**A one-covariate MAIC by hand.** *(Computation.)* An index trial has four patients with a single covariate
$x\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}$ (one per value) and a comparator that reports mean $\bar x_{BC}=0.5$. Write the
balance equation $\sum_i(x_i-0.5)e^{\beta(x_i-0.5)}=0$, solve for $\beta$ numerically to three decimal
places, report the normalized weights summing to $4$, verify that the weighted mean is $0.5$, and compute
the effective sample size and the variance inflation factor. Comment on how the ESS would change if the
target were $\bar x_{BC}=1.5$ instead.
:::

::: {#exr-maic-secondmoment}
**Balancing a variance.** *(Computation.)* Continue @exm-maic-twocov and suppose the comparator also
reports the variance of $x_1$. Write the augmented feature map $\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})=(x_1,x_2,x_1^2)$
and the three balance equations. (a) Show that, because $x_1^2=1$ for every index patient, the third
equation holds automatically if the reported variance is $0.75$ and has no solution if it is $0.5$.
(b) Explain why a variance constraint on a covariate that takes only two values carries no new
information. (c) Show that adding any feasible balance constraint cannot decrease the minimized objective
$H(\mathbf{w}^{*})$ of @eq-maic-entropy.
:::

::: {#exr-maic-logit}
**Recovering the logistic weights.** *(Computation.)* Using @thm-maic-logistic-ipw-equiv, suppose a logistic
trial-membership model has fitted coefficients $\tilde\alpha=0.3$ and
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=(0.8,-0.4)$. Write the inverse-odds weight as a function of $\mathbf{x}$,
identify the MAIC parameter $\boldsymbol{\beta}$, and explain in one paragraph why the MAIC method of
moments and logistic maximum likelihood give the same weight *form* but generally different *fitted
values* when the comparator supplies only covariate means.
:::

::: {#exr-maic-ess-majorization}
**The ESS and majorization.** *(Challenge.)* Show that among all nonnegative weight vectors with a fixed
sum, the effective sample size @eq-maic-ess is maximized uniquely by the uniform vector, and more generally
that if $\mathbf{w}'$ majorizes $\mathbf{w}$ (the sorted partial sums of $\mathbf{w}'$ dominate those of
$\mathbf{w}$, with equal total, so $\mathbf{w}'$ is the more concentrated or lopsided vector) then
$\mathrm{ESS}(\mathbf{w}')\le\mathrm{ESS}(\mathbf{w})$. Deduce @thm-maic-ess-bound as the special case
where $\mathbf{w}'$ concentrates all weight on one coordinate. (Hint: $\mathbf{w}\mapsto\sum_i w_i^2$ is
Schur-convex, meaning it never decreases when weight is shifted from a smaller coordinate to a larger one;
a Schur-convex function is therefore smallest at the most equal vector and largest at the most concentrated,
which is exactly what the ESS bound records.)
:::

::: {#exr-maic-bias-decomp}
**($\star$) Decomposing the adjustment.** *(Proof.)* In @exm-maic-twocov, replace the conditional benefit $4+x_1$ by the
general form $b_0+b_1x_1+b_2x_2$ and the comparator mean by a general $(\bar x_{1},\bar x_{2})$ inside the
square. Derive a closed-form expression for the MAIC-adjusted benefit $\hat d_{AC}^{\mathrm{MAIC}}$ in
terms of $b_0,b_1,b_2$ and the target means, prove that it equals the true comparator-population benefit
$b_0+b_1\bar x_1+b_2\bar x_2$ for *any* weights achieving moment balance (not only the entropy weights),
and conclude that on the identity scale with a linear benefit the choice of balancing objective affects
the variance (through the ESS) but not the point estimate. Explain how this exact-on-the-mean property
fails on the logit scale, connecting to the higher-moment discussion of @sec-maic-moment and
@def-non-collapsibility.
:::

::: {#exr-maic-sandwich-vs-naive}
**($\star$) Naive versus sandwich variance.** *(Challenge.)* Consider the stacked estimating equations @eq-maic-estfun for a
single-arm weighted mean (drop the $C$ block). Write the $2\times 2$ block-triangular Jacobian $A$ in the
scalar-covariate case, invert it explicitly, and show that the asymptotic variance of $\hat\mu_A$ has the
fixed-weight term (which reduces to $\sigma^2/\mathrm{ESS}$ when the conditional mean is constant) *plus*
a correction attributable to estimating
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$. Identify the data configuration in which the correction vanishes (so that the naive
and sandwich variances agree) and interpret it: it is the case where the outcome is uncorrelated, within
the weighting, with the balancing covariate. Relate your finding to the remark following
@thm-maic-sandwich-variance: when is the correction negative, and can it be positive?
:::
